Senses.Explanation: The graphs mean “carry,” “board,” and “fellow”: “a board-carrying fellow.” The records themselves repeatedly connect the name with seeing only one side. The stock line says, “Xu Six carries a board and sees only one side,” and a later comment states directly, “Each sees one side: precisely a board-carrying fellow.” In the Muezhou case, Muezhou calls to a monk; when the monk turns his head, Muezhou calls him a board-carrying fellow. Xuedou and Huanglong then give opposing comments on why the monk should or should not receive the name, and a later speaker judges that each commentator sees one side. The label is not confined to that case. One address calls both contentment at a rich feast and fear in a thorn thicket instances of the same name. Another says that explaining five ranks, three mysteries, divisions, reality, and expedients “only makes a board-carrying fellow,” then asks how the matter can be raised whole. A later direct naming formula says, “Learning without awakening is called overbearing pride; awakening without learning is called a board-carrying fellow.” The entry reports these recorded applications and the texts’ own one-sidedness wording.
Senses.Note: The headword occurs 193 times in 90 allowlisted texts; the shorter “carry a board” form occurs 589 times in 186 texts. “Xu Six carries a board and sees only one side” occurs 5 times in 5 texts. Three occurrences in two texts ask why the turned monk is or is not called a board-carrying fellow. The recurring Muezhou exchange and later comments must be kept distinct: Muezhou supplies the name in the case; Xuedou, Huanglong, and later speakers argue over its application.

Occurrences.Kwic: 各見一邊，正是擔板漢。今晚或云：『雲門與麼道，也是擔板漢。』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baiyu, an evening address commenting on Xuedou and Huanglong: “Each sees one side, precisely a board-carrying fellow. Tonight, if someone says, ‘Yunmen speaking this way is also a board-carrying fellow’...”

Occurrences.Kwic: 諸方道。徐六擔板只見一邊。尚書不學牆面。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Book of Serenity commentary records two sayings: “Xu Six carries a board and sees only one side,” and “An officer who does not study faces a wall.” This unique short-form witness omits the final graph for “fellow” but supplies the corpus's recurrent one-side description of the full headword.

Occurrences.Kwic: 睦州和尚一日喚僧云：『大德！』僧回首，州云：『擔板漢。』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Muezhou case is raised: Muezhou calls “Worthy one!”; the monk turns his head, and Muezhou says, “Board-carrying fellow.” The exchange has multiple speakers, so the occurrence speaker remains null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 有學無悟謂之增上慢，有悟無學謂之擔板漢。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Dongshan Meixi Du, presented to layman Li Zuiliang: “Learning without awakening is called overbearing pride; awakening without learning is called a board-carrying fellow.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 坐豐美筵席，唱太平曲子，無不爽心稱快，也是擔板漢。住荊棘叢林，入虎狼群隊，無不戰驚受懼，也是擔板漢。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhean Fan gives opposed applications: delight at a rich feast is called a board-carrying fellow, and fear amid thorns, tigers, and wolves is also called one.

Occurrences.Kwic: 只成擔板漢。此事如何舉得全？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The same recorded sayings says that enumerating ranks, mysteries, divisions, reality, and expedients “only makes a board-carrying fellow,” then asks, “How can this matter be raised whole?”

Senses.Explanation: Both graphs name bearing a load: to shoulder or carry it. One exact verse names physical firewood carried on one shoulder until the carrying pole breaks. Far more often the Chan corpus leaves the load unstated or names responsibility, succession, inheritance, or teaching. Productive forms include “shoulder it successfully” (擔荷得), “shoulder with the whole body” (全身擔荷), and “shoulder it on one shoulder” (一肩擔荷). Yuanwu lists “accept successfully, shoulder successfully, head toward successfully, carry out successfully” (承當得，擔荷得，趣向得，行履得). Jiufeng Daoqian says, “knowing to accept and shoulder it inwardly is inner succession” (知向裏許承當擔荷，是為內紹), then says one must see “the person with no accepting and the person with no shouldering” before reaching “one color” (須見無承當底人，無擔荷底人，始得同一色). The same load-bearing verb therefore spans physical cargo and the corpus's dominant responsibility and lineage deployments. Literal and figurative loads do not make the act of shouldering two lexical things.
Senses.Note: The headword occurs 868 times in 243 allowlisted texts. The former physical/figurative targets name the same load-bearing action and are merged. Explicit firewood is rare; responsibility and lineage language dominate. Attested formations include “one who shoulders” (擔荷者), “shoulder successfully” (擔荷得), “shoulder with the whole body” (全身擔荷), “shoulder on one shoulder” (一肩擔荷), “accept and shoulder” (承當擔荷), and “unable to shoulder” (擔荷不起). The reversed form “carry a load” (荷擔) belongs to the family but does not create another referent.

Occurrences.Kwic: 驀然有箇承當得。擔荷得。趣向得。行履得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu Keqin's own discourse record, under 'addresses to the assembly, six.' He enumerates four parallel successful verbs: accepting, shouldering, heading toward, and carrying out.

Occurrences.Kwic: 少林演妙訣。唯許神光擔荷。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu Keqin's own discourse record, under 'minor addresses, three.' The sentence says, 'Shaolin expounded the subtle key; only Shenguang was allowed to shoulder it.' Shenguang is the name used here for the second ancestor.

Occurrences.Kwic: 眾中有全身擔荷者出來與山僧相見。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Records of Ancient Worthies (古尊宿語錄), the speaker calls: 'if among the assembly there is one who shoulders it with the whole body, come out and meet this mountain monk.' The local head pointer is a generic collected-sayings heading and does not securely identify the speaker, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 歷代祖師有擎山舉鼎之力，也擔荷不起
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the record of Sanyi Yu (三宜盂禪師), under his Yunmen Xiansheng Monastery addresses, the speaker says: 'the ancestral teachers of successive generations had the strength to lift mountains and raise tripods, yet could not shoulder it.' The master is named by the text but lacks an exact roster spelling.

Occurrences.Kwic: 知向裏許承當擔荷。是為內紹。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The governing head in the Five Lamps Compendium (五燈會元) is Jiufeng Daoqian. Asked about inner succession, he says, 'knowing to accept and shoulder it inwardly is inner succession.' This is the corpus's clearest explicit classification involving the headword.

Occurrences.Kwic: 須見無承當底人。無擔荷底人。始得同一色。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Continuation of Jiufeng Daoqian's same exchange: 'one must see the person with no accepting and the person with no shouldering; only then does one reach one color.' Kept separately because it supplies the text's direct contrast to the preceding definition.

Occurrences.Kwic: 有力量者進前來一肩擔荷得去
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The governing head in the Complete Book of the Five Lamps (五燈全書) is Xueqiao Yuanxin. He calls, 'those with strength, come forward and shoulder it on one shoulder.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 爭得盧公賽子雲，一肩擔荷柴衝折。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The verse says, ‘How could Master Lu rival Ziyun? Carrying firewood on one shoulder, the carrying pole breaks.’ This is the sole researched exact-headword witness with explicit physical cargo.

Senses.PreferredTarget: carry snow to fill a well
AlternateTargets: fill a well by carrying snow
Senses.Explanation: Literally, "carry snow to fill a well" (擔雪填井): the load melts while the well remains unfilled. Chan records use the concrete impossibility as a compact appraisal of ineffective religious display and effort. Baishan applies it separately to "pick it up and immediately use it" (拈來便用), to question-and-answer exchanges in an enumeration beside "talking mysteries, drawing a cake to satisfy hunger" (談玄說妙，畫餅充饑), and to trying to pass through by silent stillness, contrasted with trying to state it in words as "proving a turtle to be a soft-shelled turtle" (證龜成鱉). Tian'an calls sitting Chan like carrying snow to fill a well and rhymingly calls composing poetry kneading snow into a ball (捏雪成團). Yinyuan pairs the phrase with trying to fill a net by blowing (吹網欲滿) and says that even ages of such actions have no place. The Zen-specific deployment is a verdict applied not to an ordinary futile chore but to recognizable Chan-scene responses—silence, words, questions and answers, sitting, gestures, and other attempted displays.
Senses.Note: The exact phrase has 32 hits in 28 allowlisted texts. No formula self-definition was found; its predicates emerge from enumerations and explicit similes. Three distinct Baishan deployments are retained because they assign the image to different response shapes; independent Tian'an and Yinyuan passages establish broader use.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若道拈來便用，何異擔雪填井。若道總不與麼，也是證龜成鱉。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Baishan compares picking up and immediately using the whisk to carrying snow to fill a well, and the contrary response to proving a turtle a soft-shelled turtle.

Occurrences.Kwic: 拈椎豎拂，望梅止渴，談玄說玅，畫餅充饑，一問一荅，擔雪填井，行棒行喝，無事生事。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Baishan's enumeration assigns carrying snow to fill a well to one-question-one-answer exchanges amid other paired appraisals.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若以寂默通，則擔雪填井；若以語言道，則證龜成鱉。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Baishan contrasts trying to pass through by silent stillness with trying to state it through words.

Occurrences.Kwic: 坐禪者，大似擔雪填井。吟詩者，何異捏雪成團？惟有說食者卻最親切。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Tian'an compares sitting Chan to carrying snow to fill a well and composing poetry to kneading snow into a ball.

Occurrences.Kwic: 所作所為，擔雪填井，吹綱欲滿，縱經塵劫，無有是處。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yinyuan pairs the phrase with blowing into a net in hopes of filling it and extends the appraisal across ages.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, “body or substance” and “exposed”: “body or substance exposed.” The compound occurs 646 times in 222 allowlisted texts. Its syntax varies: the body or constant substance is exposed, while the preceding word “whole” can make the entire body exposed. One discourse explicitly says that when feelings about holy and ordinary are exhausted, this is called “true constancy, body exposed.” Another recurrent statement says, “True constancy, body exposed, not constrained by written words.” The fixed Yunmen exchange asks, “What about when the tree withers and the leaves fall?” and answers, “Body exposed in the autumn wind.” That four-graph answer occurs 176 times in 100 texts and is repeatedly raised, versified, and questioned by later masters. Other expansions include “body exposed, imposing and evident” and “the whole body exposed.”
Senses.Note: The entry does not choose an unstated referent for 'body' in every occurrence. It records the nouns and predicates supplied by each text. 'The whole body exposed' occurs 153 times in 95 texts, and 'fully exposed, imposing and evident' occurs 61 times in 49. The direct question 'What is the body-exposed-in-autumn-wind saying?' is also attested.

Occurrences.Kwic: 有年有德復云不用愛聖聖是空名不用厭凢凢是妄立若得聖凢情盡喚作體露真常所以古者道但盡妄緣即如如佛諸人還信得及麼若信得及止宿草庵
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A Yunfeng section explicitly says that exhausting feelings about holy and ordinary is called 'true constancy fully exposed.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 大眾退後。進云：過在什麼處？師云：還我九十日飯錢來。問：樹凋葉落時如何？師云：體露金風。問：一切智通無障礙時如何？師云：埽地潑水相公來。問：隨
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Yunmen's record, an anonymous question about a withered tree and fallen leaves receives the autumn-wind answer.

Occurrences.Kwic: 何。試舉看。【二七】舉。僧問雲門。樹凋葉落時如何雲門云。體露金風。若向箇裏薦得。始見雲門為人處。其或未然。依舊只是指鹿為
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Blue Cliff case twenty-seven raises Yunmen's exchange before beginning its commentary.

Occurrences.Kwic: 審和尚以何顯道？師曰：山僧祇似鐵。乃曰：極目青天無片雲，萬象森羅全體露。若也擬議更商量，特地翻成箇露布。久立，歸堂喫茶去。上堂
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A discourse joins the reverse-order array of the ten thousand forms to 'the whole body exposed.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 聞舉少林面壁，頓悟。述二偈以呈，龍許之。住後，上堂，舉：體露堂堂，十方無󳬩礙。千聖不能傳，萬靈成頂戴。擬欲共商量，開口百
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lamp biography preserves a verse beginning 'fully exposed, imposing and evident.'
